title: How do I make a game that looks like Octopath Traveler?

posts.author: dwr7eleven
posts.body:
The reason I would like my game to look like this is because I am currently making a Spiritual Successor to Mario & Luigi in the RPG Maker MV Engine. Critics of the recent Mario & Luigi Brothership thinks that the Acquire developers should've made a Mario & Luigi that looked like Octopath, instead of the 3D Models. I like the 3D Models and Brothership's art style in general, but I too think this was a missed opportunity.
I also want my RPG Maker Game to stand out, and not look like the default assets. I wouldn't mind making these assets myself, but if possible, it would be cool if my Mario & Luigi spiritual successor looked like this. No, I will not be using any Nintendo characters.

posts.author: TheAM-Dol
posts.body:
I will say that just recommending using UE is not really a good suggestion - though accurate if you truly want to 100% emulate the style.
Simply because we all know we are here using RM because we're too dumb to figure out those more technical engines. UE is pretty dense and tough to wrap your head around. I imagine OP wants to use RM because it's user friendliness allows him to more easily make a game.
That being said; RM still is not necessarily a good answer to this.
The thing is about MV/Z3D is that it's rather bloated and performs poorly on systems. With RM not well utilizing system resources, adding in pixi filters on top as well is going to make the game even more demanding on people's systems.
You'd also need a custom filter, which you'd need to commission, and pixi filters are not cheap.
The resource Trid linked for pixi filter controller does not have a tilt-shift effect, nor does it have a bokeh effect either - tilt shift being the effect where only the middle of the frame is in focus while the foreground and background are out of focus.
1) Pixi filters cannot target "depth" of a scene. So you could only put a blur on the top of the screen and bottom, but that's not true tilt shift, since tilt shift is about the depth of the image (how close or far things are from the camera) (You can target layers, but layers never dynamically change, so even if the farthest away/lowest layer had the blur applied to it, when it moves closer to the camera, it would still be blurred as if it was far away because it's still the same layer.)
2) Bokeh is true lens defocusing, and was heavily used to create the feel of Octopath. You'll notice that (at least with professional camera lenses and not your tiny phone camera) that parts that are not in focused are not just a gaussian blur, but instead very textured in both the shape and how it alters the way the light defocuses - such as the shimmer from very bright spots in the scene. Bokeh is very complex to simulate, and as such usually is pretty taxing on system resources. Additionally, there are no bokeh pixi filters available.
For a bit of opinion, I am not sure where you heard these opinions about the art style of the Mario and Luigi games. The thing is, Octopath's style is very dreamlike with the heavy bokeh, high contrast, and tilt-shift effect.
The tilt-shift effect is fun, but tends to give every thing a "toy like" appearance. It may work for a more cartoony styled game like Mario & Luigi. You can see in the remade Link's Awakening and new Zelda: Zelda game how the tilt shift effect was used.
But overall, I don't think it meaningfully changes the game's feeling.
Basically what I am saying is that these aesthetic filters, when applied heavily seem counter to the feeling of Mario & Luigi, while applied subtlely doesn't add much to the game and therefore is not a high priority for your game's development.
If you really want to play with how the game feels through filters, it's something I would mess around with last in the development pipeline. For the time being, I'd just focus on making a fun game and learning the engine.

posts.author: SylarDean
posts.body:
'RPG Developer Bakin' can achieve the 2.5D octo look for games just by simply building your game in 3D then locking the camera at the same angle as octo's angle. The engine is extremely similar to rpg maker in how the editor works with placing assets and stuff, you can even choose to use 3D or 2D sprites/models, import your own assets, use custom stuff, it has full control over every aspect of HUD/UI so very easy to make your own within the engine itself. No limits of events, common events, variables, maps, etc. Animations uses Effekseer, so if you've experience in that.. that'll help loads. There's no hidden payments for release of games too, so you can release a commercial game no problem with no hidden costs. OH! It also makes use of C# scripting if you need scripts or custom scripts made. The devs are working on a Unity add-on for it too so you'll have access to unity for your game in Bakin eventually too.
I think the issue your gonna have tho is assets, the community is quite small so there's not many who'll do custom art, models, etc.. so expect to pay more in Bakin that you would in RPGMaker. So it might be worth you taking a look at that engine too.

posts.author: DrFreeman
posts.body:
The most graphically advanced project I've seen on RPG Maker was Project Varinsite by KyouNight (暁夜KyouNight). I read deep into her Twitter and she used
MV3D
/
MZ3D
. The plugin is based on Babylon.js. It is pretty good, but many 3D projects seem to perform very poorly on mobile devices. Here is a sample on PC:
So, it is possible to make something
like
it.
The HDR blur and the lighting bloom are going to be pretty easy. There are already plugins for them. What is going to be difficult is the 3D which I'm working on. Like everyone else told you, it is probably easier to make this with Unity or Unreal, get a template, some assets, and then slap your game onto it. For most, that works. But if you are like me, I prefer using JS and RPG Maker. Depending on your game, it might be the right tool for the job.
Warning
: Doing 3D programming is not for the feint of heart. This typically exceeds the acceptable range of most RPG maker games. At that point, you would be better off hiring someone or recruiting someone for your project. But if you are determined to build this...
Here are some options:
Like others said,
MV3D
/
MZ3D
made by CutieVirus. It is what many use for 3D projects on RPG Maker. Requires little setup.
Here is the tutorial
.
The
Rose Engine
might be able to do it, but it is going to take a while.
Chaucer
made it from the ground up. He is still regularly active on RPG Maker, I messaged him yesterday.
Rose Engine tutorial is here
. I don't think he released his MV version yet though.
Requires a lot of programming
. Another other way I can think is using Three.js; it is the most popular 3D JS Framework. I really like Three.js, but I haven't had enough time to make a plugin for it.
Requires a lot of programming
. There is another way that is possible to do it with WebAssembly (WASM) using a typical graphics pipeline which I would like to use. Then I could just stick with bread and butter C++ then convert it to JS. And it is compatible with NodeJS which means you could use parallel processing.
Requires a lot of programming
. The last way which is most likely to work, but it is the most difficult is straight WebGL. This would require making an outside program and connecting to your project similar to a bootloader. I don't really recommend this way.
Let's suppose you used MV3D because it is quick to purchase. You
setup the plugin
, you get your scene ready, and then you run into the tedious part. Mapping in 3D on RPG Maker requires a lot of patience. You have to set up the model part in note area of the map. If you've got this far then this about where I am. I have run into a few issues with 3D lighting, parallax, weather effects, physics/collision detection, and a few others. I know it is possible to make advanced games with this engine, but it takes time and a lot of effort. I might talk to some friends at ArenaNet, Bungie, EA, or Microsoft to see if they could give me a hand on some of this.
Regardless of how difficult a game is to create, if the story must be heard, then there is still work to be done.

posts.author: JohnDoeGames
posts.body:
Anyhow, I don't think changing the engine is the right step for OP. They seem to be completely new to game development, they apparently already own RPG maker and it looks like they don't have any programming experience. So every other engine will at least be as hard for them, probably even much harder.
I think the right thing to do, is to adjust the wishes and expectations. Things like MV3D can do great stuff, and would amaze most RPG maker gamers. However, if you expect the awesome things you've seen in popular games made by professional studio's and in professional 3D engines, then RPG maker will seem childish and flat.
@dwr7eleven
Are you indeed new to developing? Or at least to RPG maker? I would very much recommend to first create something that was made with just the engine as it was intended. Get used to the default commands and get the feeling of what RPG maker can or can not do.
I can tell you from experience that gameplay wise, you can stretch the limits of RPG make way, way, waaaaaaaaay beyond JRPG's, but graphics wise it is and always will be a 2D engine. You can make 3D stuff with it, which will seem 3D, but once you start using it, you notice you'll never make 3D models, but rather create flat images, but standing straight up and from different angles.
And, well... That is what makes RPG maker so strong and easy to use. With 2D images you can use everything, from doodle to photo to painting to linoleum prints... 3D models however, are... uhm... The models alone have a learning curve by itself. On top of the learning curve of the engine.
So, as I said, I don't think changing engines is the step you really need to take. I thing, if you start creating something possible first, you can always push your limits later.
If this ambitious project is going to be your first project, you will most likely fail, feel bad about your own work, and never make another game. But if you make something simple first, you will probably succeed, get positive feedback and gain the confidence to take on seemingly impossible projects.
--------------------------------
But that all being said... Let people saying "It cant be done" never ever stop you.
I created 99.9% of all my systems for 1 single reason: I thought it was impossible, so I had to try. A fine example is people asking me how to make a chess game. For years I told people it isn't possible with RPG maker, until I tried it myself... I was done in less than 2 days.
So, if you really, really want it and you think you can do it, do not let us nay naysayers hold you back. We are probably right, but all of us would be impressed, if you would proof us wrong.
